title: Paloma and the Room
premise: Orsen Nakamura, a pest controller who learned early that being forgettable keeps you safe, is called to a house where the infestation leaves fingerprints in the dust—and finds their childhood imaginary friend Paloma waiting on the porch, unchanged after thirty years. The house feeds on people who were once invisible children, and it has been keeping a room for Orsen all along. To survive, Orsen must learn the last verse of the song Paloma taught them without singing along, because singing it aloud signs you over to whatever waits inside. In the end, Orsen refuses both the room and the silence that made them prey, burning the house's ledger of names and walking out visible for the first time—while Paloma, finally remembered by someone who survived, dissolves into morning light.
about_author: W. M. Zhou is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade documenting structures no one wanted to enter. They write horror about the quiet violence of being overlooked, and live somewhere they refuse to put on record.

chapters.title: The Call Comes at Dusk
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A routine pest-control call to a house on Verrin Street that isn't on any map Orsen owns. The dispatcher's voice glitches when reading the address. Orsen goes anyway, because rent is due and being needed is safer than being noticed. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Dust
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Inside, the droppings are wrong—arranged in patterns, and small handprints pressed into attic dust, adult-sized but childlike in spacing. The homeowner, Mrs. Adeyemi, watches from the doorway and never blinks. Emotional beat: creeping wrongness beneath mundane procedure.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen counts eleven doors in a house built for eight and recounts twice; the number changes only when they stop looking. They keep the lights on, a childhood habit, and note the hallway hums like a held breath. Emotional beat: the comfort of rituals fraying.

chapters.title: Paloma on the Porch
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Leaving at midnight, Orsen finds a woman on the porch steps—Paloma, the imaginary friend from age seven, unaged, wearing the same yellow raincoat. She says, 'You kept the lights on. Good.' Orsen drives away shaking. Emotional beat: terror braided with unbearable longing.

chapters.title: What Imaginary Friends Are For
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Orsen's POV. 1990s: a neglected kid invents Paloma, who teaches them a counting song to make the shouting downstairs stop. Paloma promises: 'As long as you're nobody, nobody can hurt you.' Emotional beat: tenderness curdling into a lesson in erasure.

chapters.title: Mrs. Adeyemi's Ledger
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Returning for a follow-up, Orsen finds Mrs. Adeyemi writing names in an old ledger—children's names, including Orsen's own, dated decades ago. She claims she's just 'keeping the house's books.' Emotional beat: the horror of discovering you were always expected.

chapters.title: The Song Has Four Verses
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV (uncanny, second-person-adjacent). Paloma explains the house takes invisible children and keeps them in a room where they're finally seen forever. Three verses bind you; the fourth frees you—but only if you learn it without ever singing along. Emotional beat: seductive, poisoned care.

chapters.title: Missing Since Tuesday
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A neighborhood boy, Dev, vanishes; his mother says he 'went into the Adeyemi house to look for his brother,' missing since 1989. Police find nothing. Orsen realizes the house harvests across generations. Emotional beat: guilt—the call was never random.

chapters.title: Lights On, Doors Open
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen breaks in at night with tools and floodlights. The extra doors are real now, each opening onto the same nursery. In one, a wall of crayon drawings signed ORSEN, decades of them, done in a hand that never aged. Emotional beat: violation of the self's oldest sanctuary.

chapters.title: The Room That Waits
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen finds the room: wallpapered in names, warm as a held hand, with a small bed and a chair facing the door—as if something sits there watching, delighted. Orsen flees before the door can close. Emotional beat: claustrophobic panic.

chapters.title: Invisible Was a Choice
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, interwoven with present-day coworker Marcus. Marcus confronts Orsen: 'You've worked here nine years and I don't know your birthday.' Orsen realizes invisibility cost them every relationship. Emotional beat: grief for a life half-lived.

chapters.title: Dev Is Singing
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Through the house's windows at night, Orsen hears Dev's voice singing the first three verses, sweet and looping. Each repetition makes his voice younger. Orsen understands: the song doesn't summon the house—it unmakes you into a child worth keeping. Emotional beat: urgency sharpening to desperation.

chapters.title: Mrs. Adeyemi Confesses
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Mrs. Adeyemi was once a kept child who bargained her way out by becoming the house's bookkeeper, feeding it names so hers stayed closed. 'Justice here isn't law,' she says. 'It's accounting.' Emotional beat: pity and revulsion for a survivor turned collaborator.

chapters.title: The Fourth Verse Exists
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma admits she was the first kept child, sent out as bait because she loved Orsen enough to want company—or so the house made her believe. The fourth verse was torn from the ledger. Only someone the house wants can read what remains. Emotional beat: betrayal and broken devotion.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen deliberately stops hiding—files reports, calls attention, makes themselves loudly visible—to become worthless to the house. It backfires: the house escalates, taking Marcus's name into the ledger instead. Emotional beat: strategy collapsing into fury.

chapters.title: Breaking the Books
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen and Marcus raid the house for the ledger. Doors multiply; the nursery follows them through rooms. Marcus reads names aloud to unbind them while Orsen searches for the torn page. Emotional beat: defiant momentum, rising stakes.

chapters.title: What the House Wants With You
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The house speaks through Paloma: it doesn't eat children—it collects witnesses, adults who saw too much as kids and chose silence. Orsen wasn't called to exterminate pests. Orsen was called home. Emotional beat: the trap revealed as identity itself.

chapters.title: Singing Along
chapters.summary: Climax part one, Orsen's POV. Cornered in the waiting room, Orsen hears the fourth verse whispered from the walls—and catches themselves humming along, fingers tapping the rhythm, body signing over. Marcus screams their name to break the trance. Emotional beat: the self almost surrendered.

chapters.title: The Last Verse, Un sung
chapters.summary: Climax part two, Orsen's POV. Orsen learns the verse by heart and holds it behind their teeth—knowing it fully, giving it nothing—while reciting every name in the ledger aloud, making the invisible children witnessed without being owned. The house begins to scream in wallpaper. Emotional beat: white-knuckle triumph of refusal.

chapters.title: Fire Takes the Accounting
chapters.summary: Climax part three, Orsen's POV. Orsen burns the ledger in the nursery; the doors collapse inward like exhaled breath. Mrs. Adeyemi chooses to stay with her book, whispering names as the flames take them both. Dev walks out older than he went in. Emotional beat: cathartic destruction, justice outside any court.

chapters.title: Visible
chapters.summary: Resolution, Orsen's POV. Weeks later, Orsen gives Marcus their real birthday, calls their estranged sister, lets a coworker take their photo. Being seen hurts. Being seen is survivable. The Verrin Street lot stays empty except for daffodils no one planted. Emotional beat: fragile, chosen openness.

chapters.title: One Verse Left Over
chapters.summary: Final coda, Orsen's POV. On a rainy night, Orsen finds yellow raincoat fabric folded on their own porch—no note, no footprints. Somewhere far off, a child's voice hums three verses and stops, waiting. Orsen leaves the porch light on anyway, and does not sing. Emotional beat: bittersweet vigilance, love with teeth.
